source_supported_observation: The theory is selected by the relaxation times and a switch delta: CD with both times zero and delta = 0, LS with tau0 > 0 and delta = 1, GL with tau1 >= tau0 > 0 and delta = 0.
The boundary is the plane z = 0 with the positive z-axis inside the elastic medium; the wave travels along x and all variables are independent of y.
The text states that the P wave is affected by the thermal field while the SV wave remains unaffected.
Heat sources, external forces and body forces are assumed absent, and the motion is a small-amplitude plane wave in a homogeneous isotropic thermally conducting solid.
Boundary conditions are sigma_zz = sigma_xz = dT/dz = 0 at z = 0, that is a stress-free and thermally insulated surface.
For a surface effect the potentials must decay with distance from the boundary, which requires im1 and im2 to be imaginary and forces the constants A2, A4 and A6 to vanish.

source_supported_observation: Title and abstract describe propagation and attenuation of Rayleigh waves in a generalized thermoelastic half-space with a stress-free plane boundary.
Constitutive relation (2) represents Lord-Shulman theory with epsilon = 1 and Green-Lindsay theory with epsilon = 0, subject to tau1 >= tau0 >= 0.
The plane z = 0 is the surface of the half-space occupying z > 0, and the motion is restricted to the x-z plane with all quantities independent of y.
The biquadratic (12) yields two complex dilatational velocities named qP and qT, while the shear velocity beta in (6) is real so the shear wave propagates without decay.
A homogeneous thermally conducting isotropic medium is considered with no body forces and no thermal sources; the relaxation times satisfy tau1 >= tau0 >= 0.
The isothermal surface conditions are sigma_zz = 0, sigma_zx = 0 and T = 0 at z = 0, which lead to the dispersion equation (18).

With eta = 0 and Gamma_11 = 1 equation (18) reduces to (2-h)^2 = -4 q1 q3, the classical elastic Rayleigh secular equation; roots of the rationalized polynomial are checked against (18) to remove spurious ones.
notes: Reduction check plus internal consistency; not an experimental validation.

Velocity decreases and attenuation increases with frequency; for MHz to GHz waves velocity falls and attenuation rises with thermal conductivity; both velocity and attenuation increase with thermal expansion.

source_supported_observation: Stress depends on strain, electric field and magnetic field, while electric displacement and magnetic induction depend on strain, electric field and magnetic field, giving full magneto-electromechanical coupling.
Material parameters are fitted as power series in z/h and boundary conditions are embedded through a rectangular window function whose derivative produces Dirac deltas.
Traction-free conditions are sigma_zz = sigma_xz = sigma_yz = 0 at z = 0,h; electric and magnetic open circuit means D_z = B_z = 0 and short circuit means phi = psi = 0 at z = 0,h.
The coupled governing equations for U, W, X and Y are reduced with a Legendre polynomial expansion over [0,h] and turned into a matrix equation.
The full Lamb spectrum of a steel plate is compared with a spectral collocation method from the literature, and the curves are reported to agree well, which validates the approach and program.

Title and abstract concern propagating and non-propagating Lamb-like waves in a functionally graded piezoelectric spherical curved plate.
notes: MDPI text layer repeats a peer-review version of pages; both copies were read.

source_supported_observation: The material is a functionally graded piezoelectric material whose parameters vary in the r direction, fitted as f(r) = f(l)*(r/h)^l for an orthotropic plate polarized in the thickness direction.
A spherical curved plate is described in spherical coordinates (r, theta, phi) with inner radius a, outer radius b, thickness h and radius-thickness ratio eta = b/h.
Equation (7b) is independent and represents the SH wave, while the other three equations are coupled and correspond to the Lamb-like wave that is solved here.

Surfaces at r = a,b are traction free or mechanically fixed; the electric circuit is open (D_r = 0) or closed (phi = 0); a rectangular window function embeds these conditions in the governing equations.
Field quantities are expanded in Legendre polynomials over [a,b], integrated against the complex conjugate basis, and recast as the eigenvalue problem (12) with complex wave numbers k.

A steel spherical plate with eta = 100 and h = 1 mm is compared with Quintanilla et al. spectral collocation results, and an SH wave in a homogeneous GaAs plate is compared with analytical literature results; both agree.
notes: Two independent literature comparisons.

source_supported_observation: FGPM examples use eta = 10 and a = 9 mm with Ba2NaNb5O15 and PZT-4 constants from Table 1; the GaAs verification uses C11 = 118.8 GPa, C44 = 59.4 GPa, rho = 5307 kg/m3 and h = 1 mm.

The complete spectrum contains a finite number of real branches and infinitely many imaginary and complex branches, with real and imaginary branches in opposite-sign pairs and complex ones in conjugate quadruples.
Non-propagating phase velocity increases with frequency and exceeds the propagating velocity, for example the fifth complex branch is above 6 at fh = 3-4 while real branches stay below 2.
The electric circuit affects complex branches more than real ones, and two propagating modes below the first cut-off frequency vanish under the mechanically fixed condition.
At Omega = 1.21019 the complex branch has Psi = 0.21937 - 0.02803i and at Omega = 1.21815 the real branch has Psi = 0.19264.
Only the Lamb-like coupled system is analysed; the independent SH equation (7b) is explicitly excluded from the study.
The FGPM examples use a single radius-thickness ratio (eta = 10) and truncation order M = 30, with convergence demonstrated but no error bounds reported.
The eigenvalue problem is solved with the Mathematica Eigenvalues routine; governing equations and material tables are given but the code is not supplied.
